page: Oracle Cloud Infrastructure VM.Standard.E3.Flex.64-256 is a compute-oriented virtual machine configuration powered by AMD EPYC 7742 processors. Built on the x86_64 architecture, this instance features 64 physical cores and 128 vCPUs with two threads per core, running at a base clock speed of 2.25 GHz. Dedicated CPU allocation ensures that all 128 execution threads receive uncontended processing capacity without resource sharing across tenants.

The instance provides 256.0 GB of system memory, establishing a 1:2 vCPU-to-RAM ratio with 2.0 GB of memory per core. The configuration includes zero GPUs and does not bundle local disk storage, meaning persistent storage must be provisioned via external cloud storage volumes. Network connectivity is supported with one complimentary public IPv4 address.

With its high core count and 1:2 memory ratio, the server delivers high multi-threaded parallel throughput. The absence of local solid-state drives makes it suitable for stateless or remotely stored workloads, while the high thread count offers compute density for batch processing, continuous integration pipelines, video transcoding, and horizontally scaled application serving.
description: Oracle Cloud Infrastructure VM.Standard.E3.Flex.64-256 is a compute-focused instance delivering 128 vCPUs and 64 physical cores powered by AMD EPYC 7742 processors on the x86_64 architecture. Operating at 2.25 GHz with dedicated allocation and two threads per core, it provides consistent processing capacity across extensive multi-threaded tasks. The system is equipped with 256.0 GB of RAM, offering a 1:2 vCPU-to-memory ratio of 2.0 GB per thread. The configuration includes no integrated GPU hardware and provides no local disk storage, requiring external block storage for persistent data needs. One complimentary public IPv4 address is included. This resource balance makes the instance efficient for compute-dense parallel tasks, distributed compilation, batch processing, CI/CD workloads, and stateless application tiers where thread throughput takes precedence over local storage.
